clue.text: The weak spot in the understanding of ancient Greek

blocks.note: the Greek hero of the Trojan War
read as under-standing: the part of the foot you stand on

explanation.surface: A scholar admits a gap in their knowledge of classical Greek.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Understanding' must be split as under-standing, the thing beneath you as you stand; the clue gives the body part before its owner.
explanation.definitionFit: Achilles was vulnerable only at his heel, so the phrase is the standard idiom for a single fatal vulnerability.

clue.text: Severe, the south wind to the quarter

blocks.note: Auster is the Latin name for the south wind
east is one quarter of the compass

explanation.surface: A harsh weather report: a south wind blowing toward one compass point.
explanation.walkthrough: Compass points are quarters, so 'quarter' can give N, S, E or W; here it is E.
explanation.definitionFit: Austere means stern, strict and plain, which matches severe in manner or style.

clue.text: Henry takes Alfonso's queen —the beast!

blocks.note: Hy is an old abbreviation for Henry
Ena, Victoria Eugenie, was queen consort of Alfonso XIII of Spain

explanation.surface: In a chess game, Henry captures his opponent Alfonso's queen and is called a brute.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Takes' and 'queen' suggest chess, but Alfonso is the Spanish king whose wife was known as Ena.
explanation.definitionFit: The hyena is a wild carnivorous animal of Africa and Asia, so it is one kind of beast.

clue.text: Raises handle to make way for elevator

blocks.note: to raise is to lift
a haft is the handle of a knife or axe

explanation.surface: Someone raises a handle to clear a route for a lift.
explanation.definitionFit: A lift shaft is the vertical passage in a building in which an elevator travels up and down.

clue.text: Reimbursements claimed appear to be unknown

indicators.note: the claim is that these words seem, when said, like something else entirely

blocks.note: in algebra x stands for an unknown, and several are x's

explanation.surface: An expense claim looks suspiciously vague.
explanation.walkthrough: Exes is informal British for expenses. The letter x spelt out as a word is 'ex', so its plural is EXES.
explanation.definitionFit: Exes is short for expenses, the costs an employee claims back from an employer.

clue.text: Where there's capital provision for cornering "loudspeakers

definitions.text: Where there's capital provision for cornering "loudspeakers

blocks.note: surface reading: a city provides for fitting loudspeakers into corners
setter's reading: Speakers' Corner, the London spot where loud public speakers address crowds

explanation.walkthrough: Speakers' Corner is a famous corner of a London park where anyone may make a public speech.
explanation.definitionFit: The London park holds Speakers' Corner, the capital's traditional site for open-air soapbox oratory.

clue.text: Causes sensation in part of German city

indicators.note: taking part of a phrase means the letters are read from within the run of words

blocks.note: read across the end of the first word and start of the second

explanation.surface: Something makes a stir in one district of a German city.
explanation.definitionFit: Essen is an industrial city in the Ruhr region of western Germany.

clue.text: Head badly torn by supporter?

indicators.note: doing something badly means doing it wrong, so these letters end up out of their right order

blocks.note: taken as written
rent is the past participle of rend, to tear

explanation.surface: Someone's head was badly injured by a fan, it seems.
explanation.definitionFit: An adherent is a follower who sticks to a party or cause, so is a backer of it.

clue.text: Dangerous time for King Charles on the river

blocks.note: CR is Carolus Rex, Latin for King Charles
the Isis is the name of the Thames at Oxford

explanation.surface: A perilous moment for a king boating on the Thames.
explanation.definitionFit: A crisis is a point of acute danger or difficulty, a critical moment needing action.

clue.text: City with a day on the side for sport

definitions.text: City with a day on the side for sport

blocks.clueFragment: City with a day on the side for sport
blocks.note: surface reading: a town that keeps a spare day for games
setter's reading: a football side (team) whose name is a weekday, Wednesday

explanation.surface: A town sets aside a day every week for playing games.
explanation.walkthrough: Sheffield Wednesday is an English football club, so this city has a day of the week in the name of its team.
explanation.definitionFit: SHEFFIELD is the Yorkshire city whose football club is called Sheffield Wednesday, a weekday attached to a sporting team.

clue.text: Old French bishop in senior section of bishopric

indicators.note: one thing placed in another means the bishop's name sits inside the abbreviation for senior

blocks.note: Sr is the standard abbreviation for senior
Odo, bishop of Bayeux, half-brother of William the Conqueror

explanation.surface: A medieval French bishop held a high post in a church diocese.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old French bishop' sounds like a description, but it names one man, the Norman bishop of Bayeux.
explanation.definitionFit: The Church of England diocese of Sodor and Man has two named parts, and Sodor is one of them.

clue.text: Order, please ! Pass by !

indicators.note: as a command, Order means arrange anew, so the following word's letters are put into a new sequence

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A chairman calls a meeting to order and then urges members to move along.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Order, please!' reads as a call for quiet, but 'Order' is a command to rearrange the word that follows.
explanation.definitionFit: Time is said to elapse when it goes past, so the verb matches the phrasal verb for slipping away.

clue.text: Bridges causing trouble in the works

blocks.note: first meaning: things that span a gap
second meaning: the tools in the idiom about throwing one into the works

explanation.surface: Faulty bridges are holding up production at a factory.
explanation.walkthrough: The first sense reads the word as 'span-ners', things that span; the second is the British idiom 'a spanner in the works', meaning a disruption.
explanation.definitionFit: A bridge spans a river, so it is one kind of spanner, while thrown spanners proverbially wreck machinery.

clue.text: The EEC is one!

blocks.note: surface reading: the European Community is a single united body
setter's reading: the EEC of 1977 had nine member states, so it is an example of a group of nine

explanation.surface: A proud claim that the European Economic Community stands united.
explanation.walkthrough: When this puzzle appeared in 1977, the European Economic Community had nine members.
explanation.definitionFit: An ennead is a set or group of nine, from the Greek for nine, matching the community's membership then.

clue.text: Refinements provided by French resort on new site

indicators.note: making something new means changing its form, so the letters of the next word are set out afresh

blocks.note: the Riviera city
taken as written

explanation.surface: A smart Riviera resort is opening a new hotel with every refinement.
explanation.definitionFit: Niceties are fine details or subtleties of manners, small polish that marks sophistication.

clue.text: Appropriate means of tack, tackling a nut-case?

definitions.note: the answer is an adjective meaning mad; the clue gives a noun for a mad person

blocks.note: setter's reading: hardtack is a dry biscuit, and biscuits of that kind are this
setter's reading: the tool used to break open a nut
surface reading: someone who is mad

explanation.surface: A question about how best to deal with a lunatic.
explanation.walkthrough: Three senses meet: dry biscuits (tack is ship's biscuit), the nutcracking tool, and the informal British word for mad.
explanation.definitionFit: In informal British speech someone who is crackers is mad, which is what a nut-case is.

clue.text: Dare to measure up in variety

indicators.note: in a down entry, going up means the word is read from bottom to top
one part placed in another means it sits within the word for variety

blocks.note: an ell is an old unit of length
change gives variety, as in 'a change is as good as a rest'

explanation.surface: Someone is urged to prove themselves amid a varied field.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Measure up' looks like a single phrase, but the two words are split: a measure, then the signal to turn it round.
explanation.definitionFit: To challenge someone is to dare them to do something, a provocation that tests their nerve.

clue.text: These nationalists like Walter

definitions.note: the answer is an adjective, as in Scottish Nationalists

blocks.note: Sir Walter Scott, the novelist
the suffix -ish means like or somewhat

explanation.surface: A comparison of political campaigners to a man named Walter.
explanation.walkthrough: The Scottish National Party campaigns for Scotland's independence; -ish attached to Scott means 'like Scott'.
explanation.definitionFit: Members of the Scottish National Party are called Scottish Nationalists, so the adjective identifies those nationalists.

clue.text: Second course for this man of course

blocks.note: a tick is a moment, as in 'just a tick'
a tack is a sailing boat's course

explanation.surface: A sailor plans another heading at sea.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Of course' looks like a casual phrase, but it means of the racecourse. A tick-tack man is a bookmaker's signaller at British race meetings, sending odds by arm movements.
explanation.definitionFit: Tick-tack is the hand-signal code bookies use at racetracks, so its practitioner is a man of the racecourse.

clue.text: Complete mishit—-bad

blocks.note: in golf, to top the ball is to hit it above centre, a bad shot
food that has gone off is bad

explanation.surface: A golfer's shot was a total disaster.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Complete' looks like an adjective modifying mishit, but it is the verb that defines.
explanation.definitionFit: To top off is to finish something or round it off with a final touch.

clue.text: One seeming to pray for reform of main street

indicators.note: to reform something is to reshape it, so the letters of these words are rebuilt into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
St is the standard abbreviation for street

explanation.surface: A pious campaigner prays that the high street will be redeveloped.
explanation.walkthrough: The praying mantis holds its forelegs folded as if in prayer.
explanation.definitionFit: The insect is called the praying mantis because its raised front legs resemble hands clasped in prayer.

clue.text: Hide directions to island

blocks.note: two compass points, south and east
the Greek island

explanation.surface: A secret set of instructions for reaching an island.
explanation.definitionFit: To secrete something is to conceal it in a hidden place.

clue.text: Quiet at disturbances by country lovers

blocks.note: p (piano) is the musical marking for quiet
taken as written
riots are violent public disturbances

explanation.surface: Calm is restored after rioting by people from rural areas.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Country lovers' suggests rustic romance, but here the country is the nation.
explanation.definitionFit: A patriot is someone who loves their nation, so the plural noun fits people devoted to their homeland.

clue.text: Back-list for reference. Dig it in one?

blocks.note: first meaning: the alphabetical list of topics at the back of a book
second meaning: the finger you would poke someone with

explanation.walkthrough: A dig is a poke, and the forefinger is the one you prod with; the question mark flags the playful second sense.
explanation.definitionFit: A book's back-of-volume list of page references is its index, and the forefinger is the index finger.

clue.text: Endless wild acclaim for such verses

definitions.note: the answer is an adjective describing the verses

indicators.note: without an end means the final letter of the next word is dropped
something wild is out of control, so the remaining letters are thrown into disorder

blocks.note: acclaim with its last letter removed

explanation.surface: A poet's lines win rapturous unending applause.
explanation.definitionFit: Alcaic describes a Greek lyric stanza form named after the poet Alcaeus, so it qualifies verses written in it.

clue.text: She can put up articles on each side

indicators.note: in a down entry, putting something up means it is read from the bottom upward
pieces placed on each side of another flank it, so it ends up enclosed between them

blocks.note: a tin is a can
two indefinite articles, a and a

explanation.surface: A woman who can display goods on both sides of her stall.
explanation.definitionFit: Anita is a woman's first name, so a female 'she' in crossword terms.

clue.text: Prove right according to .metric system

blocks.note: surface reading: checking that measurements in metres are correct
setter's reading: the metre of verse, which a line fits when it has the right rhythm

explanation.walkthrough: The stray dot is on the printed page. A line of poetry scans when its stresses fit the metre.
explanation.definitionFit: Verse that scans has correct rhythm, matching the poem's pattern of stressed and unstressed syllables.

clue.text: Discover note concealed by addict

indicators.note: something concealed by another is covered over by it, so one part sits inside the other

blocks.note: to discover is to find
E is a musical note

explanation.surface: Someone learns that a message was hidden by a drug user.
explanation.walkthrough: E goes inside FIND to make FIEND.
explanation.definitionFit: A fiend can be an enthusiast or addict, as in 'dope fiend' or 'fresh-air fiend', someone hooked on something.

clue.text: In gaining money I have a motive

blocks.note: taken as written
a cent is a small coin
the contraction I've

explanation.surface: Someone admits that making money gives them a reason to act.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gaining' tells you the first word picks up the coin right after it, and the contraction I've follows.
explanation.definitionFit: An incentive is something that encourages action, so it is a reason or spur for doing something.

clue.text: It shows our sterling worth

blocks.note: surface reading: something that proves our excellent character
setter's reading: the value of the British pound against other currencies

explanation.walkthrough: 'Sterling' reads as an adjective meaning admirable, but it is the British pound.
explanation.definitionFit: The rate quoted for converting currencies tells you what the pound is worth in foreign money.
